hints: Think about how many lymphocytes can recognise the antigen the very first time you meet it, compared to the second time after memory cells have been made.
Remember what memory B-cells quickly become on re-exposure, and how that affects both the speed of the response and the amount of antibody in the blood.
walkthrough:
**Recall the primary response**

Think of your first meeting with an antigen. You only have a tiny clone of naive B-lymphocytes with the right specific receptor.

Those few cells must first be activated, then divide many times by clonal expansion before they can make plasma cells and antibody. That is why statement 1 is true and why the primary response is slow with a low antibody peak.

**Recall the secondary response**

After the first response, you keep a large population of long-lived memory B-cells and memory T-cells specific to that same antigen.

On second exposure these many memory cells are activated immediately, so no long wait for selection and expansion. That is why statement 2 is true and why the secondary response is faster.

**Link memory cells to antibody amount**

In the secondary response, many of those memory B-cells rapidly differentiate into plasma cells.

More plasma cells means much more specific antibody produced, faster and for longer. That is why statement 3 is true, so 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.

options.A: All three statements are correct. Few specific cells make the primary slow, many memory cells make the secondary fast, and differentiation of those memory cells into plasma cells gives higher antibody levels.
options.B: This misses out statement 3, which is also true because memory cells do differentiate into many antibody-secreting plasma cells.
options.C: This misses out statement 2, which is also true because the large memory cell pool is the reason the secondary response starts so quickly.
options.D: This misses out statement 1, which is also true because the small starting number of specific naive B-lymphocytes explains the slow primary response.
